speaker_role: test-prep/consultancy marketer (admissions consulting business, 'insi Consulting' or similar, staffed partly by former AOs per claim)
commercial_incentive: Yes - repeatedly promotes a paid consulting/discovery-call service throughout the video
key_insights: Generic club membership without leadership or measurable impact (e.g. passive member of Key Club, NHS, Interact) is described as something top colleges specifically dislike

Low-commitment hobby clubs (e.g. casual chess or esports participation without competitive results or leadership) are flagged as a red flag versus building something with real depth, like founding and coaching a team to a championship

Speaker claims a part-time or full-time job is an underused, differentiating extracurricular because it demonstrates responsibility and time management, citing a Duke-specific statistic from a colleague/consultant
Frequent short-term commitments (one-off volunteer events, joining/quitting clubs) are described as signaling indecision; sustained long-term involvement is preferred

Casual social media/content creation without a clear purpose or measurable following/impact is described as hard for officers to credit; a themed, purposeful account or channel (e.g. teaching STEM topics) is preferred if backed by real engagement metrics

Advises having a 'core theme' tying coursework, activities, and interests together (e.g. a CS-intending student doing CS classes, CS clubs, and related real-world experience) so the application reads as a coherent identity

Video's summarized advice: consider getting a job, commit deeply rather than superficially to fewer activities, avoid short-term/one-off commitments, and pursue activities aligned with a coherent core theme
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker cites a claim attributed to a consultant who worked with Duke: of ~20,000 Duke applicants, only 7% had jobs, and 91% of that 7% were admitted (source and methodology not given)
Speaker's own YouTube channel cited as at 8,700 subscribers after about a year of posting, used as an example of the time content creation takes to build
General claim that there are over 30,000 high schools in the US, implying a comparable number of valedictorians
notable_or_distinctive: The cited Duke jobs/admit-rate statistic (91% admit rate among the 7% of applicants with jobs) is a specific, attention-grabbing figure presented as insider information from a consultant.
reliability_notes: The Duke statistic is unsourced and secondhand ('a consultant... told me'), not from any published Duke data, and should be treated skeptically as likely correlation-not-causation or even fabricated for marketing; video is heavily promotional for the speaker's consulting service.
